name: Vod
catalog_quote: All the Balto-Finnic languages appear to have fixed initial primary accent. ... The (nearly) extinct language Votic (Ariste 1968) appears to have secondary accents on odd-numbered syllables. Also, final syllables can take secondary accent irrespective of whether they are heavy or light, except for case suffixes, which are never accented.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding

audit.deciding_source_year: 1999 (resting on Ariste 1968; primary statement held in Ariste 1948)
audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding sentences (vdH, Hendriks & van de Weijer 1999:449, 450) found verbatim in the held chapter text (filed under arch1244/src). More importantly, the held primary Ariste 1948 Vadja keele grammatika §16 (pp. 19-20), the Estonian original of the Ariste 1968 grammar that StressTyp2 and vdH cite, states first-hand: primary stress normally on the first syllable (exceptions: a few opaque compounds like para-ika and the newest Russian loans), strong secondary stress on the 3rd (and 5th) syllable with examples carrying it on word-final odd syllables, and no evident secondary stress on case endings. That is exactly the catalog rule 10 101 1010 10101... plus the case-suffix fence the record already carries, and it independently refutes StressTyp2's primary-only decode (the 'contra' note stands). fetched sources now: Agranat 2007 (192-pp. grammar, ILING RAN open PDF) p. 33 confirms

sources.quote: p. 33: 'Ударение динамическое, несмыслоразличительное, падает на первый слог, единственное исключение paráika «сейчас», где вычленяется aika «время» и, видимо, в прошлом проклитика.' 3.1.2.2: unstressed (post-tonic, non-first) vowels tend to reduce, 'чем дальше слог стоит от ударения, тем больше редукция'. sources.citation: Rozhanskiy, Fedor. 2015. The length of final vowels with respect to case syncretism in Luuditsa Votic. Linguistica Uralica 51(2): 100-133. doi:10.3176/lu.2015.2.02
sources.quote: Instrumental study of vowel duration in disyllables; takes the initial syllable as stressed ('stressed in the initial syllable vs non-stressed final'); finds strong reduction of non-initial vowels and 'only vague traces of foot isochrony in contemporary Votic'. Nothing on secondary stress placement.
